title: Opposition to rhythm and blues in the brass bands
summary: He was resisted for bringing R&B into the street, then explains how those songs became traditional; praises Kid Howard.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Maybe jumping ahead, how were you accepted by the members of-
Yeah, I mean, you coming from what I suspect was more of a R&B, rock and roll kind of background. Yeah, yeah.

I was met with a lot of opposition. I was met with a lot of opposition on, hey, come in and play in that rhythm and blues in the street. They don't want that rhythm and blues in the street. But what you gotta look at is, when I came along and so forth and so on, there was Young Pickett, also John Brunus Senior, who was with the Tuxedo Brass Band, and Andrew Morgan and those guys. And they had, just about the same time as I introduced Second Line to Olympia, Shirley Lee's song and the rhythm and blues feel was, Come on, baby, let the good time roll. Let the good time roll. Bring new songs. You're bringing in new songs because you got new people walking and parading. Yeah. So the era of 1959 to 1965 became a transition area of rhythm and blues songs turned into traditional because they are traditional. Sure. These people have made these songs in the 50s and the 40s.
